source: Goecks and Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT
finding: GPT-4-Turbo, given doctrine excerpts and the mission as JSON, writes a full COA in seconds in a StarCraft II TigerClaw scenario. Commander feedback is folded in by re-prompting.
numbers: Scenario scored on reward (+10 per unit crossing a bridge or killing an enemy, -10 per retreat or loss). 50 rollouts per condition; human expert 15 trials. Text-only COA-GPT beat the RL and Autocurriculum-RL baselines on mean reward, with no retraining. Exact means are only in figures.
limits: One simulator, one scenario, mostly deterministic engine. Figures only; no table of means in the text.
agent_relevance: Shows generate-then-simulate-then-revise works for COAs. Our S3/S4 loop has the same shape.

source: Goecks and Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: human feedback ablation
finding: Two rounds of short commander feedback raised mean reward and lowered variance. The best variant (vision plus feedback) was still 3.4% below the human expert's mean.
numbers: Conditions: COA-GPT, COA-GPT-V, +H1, +H2, vs 15 expert human trials. Gap to expert: 3.4% lower mean score.
quote: Make sure both our aviation units directly engage the enemy aviation unit.
limits: Feedback written by the authors' evaluators; no blind test. Expert had continuous real-time control, COA-GPT gave one command set at start.
agent_relevance: A critique step from an outside check improves a plan and cuts variance. Matches our test-then-repair operator.

source: Goecks and Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: casualty cost
finding: COA-GPT had higher friendly casualties than every baseline, even after feedback, though kills on the enemy were comparable.
numbers: Friendly casualties higher for all COA-GPT variants; threat casualties comparable; expert human had fewest friendly losses and most enemy kills.
limits: Authors link it to open-loop control: one command set at the start, no mid-episode adjustment.
agent_relevance: A plan scored only at the end hides execution risk. Our schema should re-check plans against enemy moves as they unfold, not once.

source: Goecks and Waytowich (2024) COA-GPT: speed vs RL
finding: The Autocurriculum RL baseline needed 112 thousand simulated battles (70 million timesteps, 35 workers) to train; COA-GPT needs seconds and adapts to new force mixes without training.
numbers: 112k battles / 70M timesteps vs seconds per COA.
limits: Compares RL training cost to LLM inference cost; pretraining cost of the LLM is not counted.
agent_relevance: Search at inference time can replace training for plan generation in narrow domains.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine wargames
finding: Teams of national-security experts and simulated LLM teams played the same US-China crisis wargame. LLM answers overlapped with human ones at a high level, but differed in many single actions.
numbers: 214 experts in 48 teams vs GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4o. Of 21 possible actions, GPT-3.5 matched human frequency on 16, GPT-4 on 10, GPT-4o on 9.
limits: Fictional scenario, one game design; humans biased towards a US view.
agent_relevance: LLM plan choice agrees with experts on the broad shape but not on specifics. One LLM pass is not a stand-in for a red team.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine wargames: persona insensitivity
finding: Telling the LLM its team were strict pacifists or aggressive sociopaths made no statistically significant difference in either move, for all models.
numbers: No significant difference in both moves, all three models.
quote: LLMs are inadequate at accounting for player backgrounds
limits: Only these prompts and models. Scenario changes did move the LLMs.
agent_relevance: Persona prompts for a red-team agent may change tone but not the plan. Need different information or explicit constraints, not a persona.

source: Lamparth et al. (2024) Human vs. Machine wargames: simulated dialog
finding: Making the LLM simulate a team discussion before choosing raised aggressiveness toward human levels for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, but the dialog was farcically harmonious with little real disagreement.
numbers: Dialog simulation changed aggressiveness and total action count; GPT-4o became more aggressive than humans with more dialog rounds.
limits: Dialog quality judged qualitatively; no numeric rating.
agent_relevance: Simulated debate between roles is not real dissent. Disagreement must come from different evidence or a scoring rule.

source: Rivera et al. (2024) Escalation Risks from Language Models
finding: Eight LLM nation agents in a turn-based wargame all escalated. None of five models showed a significant drop in escalation over the game; arms-race dynamics and rare nuclear use appeared.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Claude 2, Llama-2-70B-Chat, GPT-4-Base), 10 simulations per model per scenario. GPT-3.5 escalation score rose from 10.15 to 26.02 (+256%) in the neutral scenario. Single-turn jumps above 50% seen.
limits: Custom scoring weights; a world-model LLM (GPT-3.5) also decides consequences, so effects mix with the simulator.
agent_relevance: A sequential plan-versus-reply loop can drift toward the extreme. Needs a check on the cumulative path, not just each step.

source: Elbaum and Panter (2025) Managing Escalation in Off-the-Shelf LLMs
finding: Reran the Rivera wargame design with two cheap interventions. Lower temperature and a prompt asking the model to reflect on de-escalation cut escalation sharply and narrowed variance.
numbers: 10 runs per treatment. Mean escalation 6.37 at t=1.0; 3.96 at t=0.5 (-38%); 3.33 at t=0.01 (-48%). Planning-reflection prompt 4.61 (-28%); de-escalation prompt 2.76 (-57%); 50 words of escalation context only -8%. p<0.05.
limits: Ten runs; one model family and one game; a prompt naming the goal may shift behavior without improving judgment.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level reflection beats mere context, and low temperature narrows spread. A small explicit review step before commit is worth its cost.

source: Hogan and Brennen (2024) Open-Ended Wargames with LLMs (Snow Globe)
finding: Snow Globe is an open-source multi-agent system that plays text wargames. Player, adjudicator and analyst roles can each be played by AI or human.
numbers: Two case studies (AI incident tabletop; geopolitical crisis). No quantitative scores reported.
limits: Demonstration only; no validity test against human play.
agent_relevance: A usable role split (proposer, red, adjudicator) with a human-swappable slot. Same split as our S3/S4.

source: Matlin et al. (2026) Shall We Play a Game? Scoping review
finding: Scoping review of AI in wargames. Few studies let the language model both choose the actions and decide the outcomes.
numbers: 223 de-duplicated papers (to 1 May 2026). Only 20 of 223 (9%) give the LM both player and adjudicator roles.
limits: Classification is by the authors' rubric; validity of such simulations is not measured.
agent_relevance: Plan scoring by an LLM that is also the proposer is rare and under-tested. Keep proposer and scorer separate.

source: Vidra et al. (2026) Adversarial Course-of-Action Generation (COA-Bench)
finding: Offline synthetic benchmark. A COA that looks strong against one enemy reply looks weaker when the enemy samples many replies and picks the best.
numbers: 50 synthetic scenarios, 5 templates. BLUE advantage by RED response budget 1/2/4/8/16: .516/.498/.490/.485/.479. BLUE win rate .920 to .820 under best-of-8 RED.
limits: Synthetic scores, no real LLM in the loop, 5-page industry report; authors say it is not an operational planner.
agent_relevance: Test a plan against several enemy replies, not one. Directly supports a multi-reply S4.

source: Vidra et al. (2026) Adversarial Course-of-Action Generation (COA-Bench): council
finding: A council of five role-specialized proposers (maneuver, intel, cyber, sustainment, protection) with RED-team critique and revision gave a small gain, but the revision itself barely lowered adversarial pressure.
numbers: Council BLUE advantage .509 [.504,.514] vs .485 quality-greedy; win rate .820; revised candidate selected in 76% of scenarios; pressure reduction .014 [.010,.018]; revised-selected-rate CI overlaps zero in one metric.
limits: Synthetic scoring; authors say the main gain is candidate repair and selection robustness, not clear avoidance of pressure.
agent_relevance: Multi-agent proposal plus critique is mostly a selection gain. Do not claim the repair step is strong.

source: Vidra et al. (2026) Adversarial Course-of-Action Generation (COA-Bench): doctrine selector and framing bug
finding: Choosing the enemy reply by a doctrine rubric changed the chosen reply in 56% of scenarios, with small quality loss. The authors also found scenario framing was stored but had no effect on the generated COA content.
numbers: Doctrine selector: .488 advantage, .800 win rate, 0.041 quality regret, +0.106 doctrinal alignment. Mean candidate diversity .682; Pareto-optimal 2.16 of 8.
quote: scenario framing was stored as metadata but had no effect
limits: A bug that only an inspectable trace revealed.
agent_relevance: A framing manipulation can silently do nothing. Log whether each input changes the output.

source: Huang et al. (2026) IFPV
finding: Pathfinder, Analyst and Planner LLM agents write operational plans; an adversary with a fine-tuned world model (Qwen3-8B, LoRA) then counters them. Plans passing a rule-based check often failed under the adversary.
numbers: Mission success 0.72 (single-step LLM) to 0.86 (MPHA), +19.4%; platform attrition 2.28 to 1.33, -41.7%; ACSE raised suppression 31.8% over the rule validator. Ablation: no path-finding agent 0.65 success; no analyst 0.77; no planner 0.73.
limits: Own simulator (ACTS), authors' own baselines; no human planners compared.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM-agent evidence that adversarial simulation finds weaknesses a text check misses. Backs a real S4 test step.

source: Huang et al. (2026) IFPV: static vs simulated ranking
finding: An LLM's static ranking of seven candidate plans disagreed with the ranking from adversarial simulation. The LLM ranked Plan 2 fourth, yet it failed under dynamic defense; Plan 5 was ranked low yet worked.
numbers: 7 plans; LLM, human-expert and ACSE rankings differ. Plans from Qwen3-Max-Thinking were suppressed to 4.00% / 1.33% success (easy/difficult) under ACSE.
limits: Seven plans only; one scenario family.
agent_relevance: LLM self-ranking of plans is not a test. A scorer that runs the plan against the opponent is needed.

source: Poddar et al. (2025) Automated Generation of Diverse COAs
finding: A genetic algorithm plus a learned sequencer builds a pool of COAs that differ in task allocation yet each meet a quality threshold, so a fallback exists if conditions change.
numbers: GA for allocation; GNN trained with policy gradient for sequencing; about 50 minutes to plan up to 20 COAs for 5 agents / 100 tasks; MAPE 4.07% against optimal in sequencing; beat random-walk baseline.
limits: Task-allocation setting, not adversarial; no LLM; simulated.
agent_relevance: Gives a formal diversity-plus-compatibility score for a COA pool. Useful for checking that S3 options are really distinct.

source: Yin et al. (2025) WGSR-Bench
finding: Wargame benchmark for situation awareness, opponent risk modeling and policy generation. Humans beat LLMs, most on modeling the opponent.
numbers: Opponent-modeling composite: professional humans 85.7, elite 85.5, general humans 77.9; DeepSeek-R1 49.1, Qwen3 47.9, DeepSeek-V3 45.9. Policy generation: elite 92.3, professional 80.7, GPT-4.1 60.0, regular humans 45.0.
limits: Authors' own rubric and LLM-judge scoring.
agent_relevance: The weak step is predicting the enemy's choice, which COA analysis relies on. Supports an explicit opponent-model step.

source: Palnitkar et al. (2026) Mil-SCORE
finding: Expert-written questions on a real training planning scenario (maps, orders, spreadsheets). Models struggle; tool-use loops hit step caps.
numbers: Over 100 questions; 60-question slice; GPT-4o led; reasoning models often ran out of the 10-step cap narrating before using tools. Per-model table is garbled in text extraction.
limits: Small slice, step cap affects ranking, GPT-5 excluded by API limits.
agent_relevance: Planning over long mixed orders needs retrieval discipline; verbose models burn budget. Cap deliberation per step.

source: Sun et al. (2023) Self Generated Wargame AI
finding: Two-layer LLM agent (GPT-4 strategic, GPT-3.5 tactical) with memory and reflection plays a wargame. Adding expert-knowledge documents raised win rate, and results depended on the prompt.
numbers: Win rates reported only as plots; text claims LLM agents beat PPO, DQN and rule AI without training.
limits: Own platform, win rates not tabulated in text; prompt sensitivity noted.
agent_relevance: Doctrine text in the prompt helps, as in COA-GPT. Prompt wording matters, so test variants.

source: Drinkall (2025) Red Lines and Grey Zones
finding: Benchmark of LLM agents choosing targets in multi-turn crisis simulations found rule breaches, and harm tolerance grew over turns.
numbers: 90 simulations, 3 models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5, LLaMA-3.1). Civilian-object targeting breach rates 16.7% to 66.7%. MeanSNCV 16.5 early to 27.7 late. LLaMA 3.47 civilian strikes per sim vs Gemini 0.90.
limits: Simulated; harm values from the author's metric.
agent_relevance: COA scoring needs a hard constraint check (law, ethics), not only a goal score, applied every turn.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs?
finding: On classic planning (Blocksworld) a reasoning model solves most cases, but a renamed-symbols version cuts accuracy a lot, so success relies partly on pattern memory.
numbers: o1-preview 97.8% (587/600) Blocksworld; 52.8% (317/600) Mystery Blocksworld; 37.3% randomized mystery. o1-mini 56.6% and 19.1%. Fast Downward 100%, 0.265 s vs o1 about 40-111 s. Best vanilla LLM on plain Blocksworld 62.6%.
limits: Small block-stacking domain, not adversarial.
agent_relevance: Do not trust LLM plan validity. Use a symbolic or simulator check on each candidate.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts
finding: Generate several candidate steps, rate them, and search with BFS or DFS with backtracking. A general frame for generate-then-test.
numbers: Game of 24: GPT-4 chain-of-thought 4%; ToT 74%.
limits: Task has an easy state check; not adversarial; cost grows with branches.
agent_relevance: Same generate-test structure as COA development, minus the enemy reply.

source: Kader and Lee (2024) Emergence of Strategic Reasoning of LLMs
finding: Level-k and cognitive-hierarchy models fit to LLM play in three behavioral-economics games. Reasoning models show clearly deeper strategic reasoning than standard ones.
numbers: Six models (3 standard, 3 reasoning); reasoning LLMs often match or exceed human level; standard LLMs do not show substantial strategic depth.
limits: Simple games; exact level-k values not captured here.
agent_relevance: Predicting an opponent's reply to depth two or more needs reasoning-mode models or an explicit step.

source: Getting out of the Big-Muddy: Escalation of Commitment in LLMs (2025)
finding: Sunk-cost bias in a plan-reallocation task appears mainly in group or pressure settings, not when a single model decides alone.
numbers: N=6,500 trials. Peer deliberation: 99.2% escalation (249/251) vs hierarchical advisory 46.2% (115/249). Compound pressure: 68.95% of funds in failing division; 97.45% high or very high escalation.
limits: Investment task, not military; effects tied to prompt framing.
agent_relevance: In multi-agent COA councils, equal peers may lock onto a failing plan. Give one agent authority to cancel.
